passages.t: The priests from Aaron to the exile
passages.happening: The sons of Levi are named, and the high priestly line runs from Aaron, the brother of Moses, generation by generation (verses 1-14), to Jehozadak, who ‘went into captivity when the LORD sent Judah and Jerusalem into exile by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar’ (verse 15). Then the three Levite clans, Gershom, Kohath and Merari, are listed (verses 16-30). Among the Kohathites stands Samuel, with his sons Joel and Abijah (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
At the center of the nine chapters the Chronicler places Levi, the tribe that served at God's house. For him worship is the heart of Israel's life, and this chapter tells the reader what the rest of the book will care about.

In the Hebrew Bible this chapter begins at 5:27, so the verse numbers differ by fifteen; the words are the same. Several names in the priestly line can be matched with events. Zadok served under David and Solomon. Hilkiah found the book of the law in Josiah's reign. Seraiah was executed by the Babylonians after the city fell. Jehozadak's son Joshua became high priest after the return, so this list is the priestly bridge from the first temple to the second. It is selective: it follows only the line of Eleazar and Zadok and passes over high priests known from Kings, such as Jehoiada, and Eli's house.
passages.later: Second Kings tells how ‘Hilkiah the high priest’ found the book of the law (2 Kings 22:8), and Ezra names Jehozadak's son ‘Jeshua son of Jozadak’ among the first to rebuild the altar (Ezra 3:2).
passages.hard:
Was Samuel a Levite or an Ephraimite?

Here Samuel appears in the Levite clan of Kohath, and his grandson Heman is a leading singer. Yet 1 Samuel introduces his father Elkanah as ‘an Ephraimite’ (1 Samuel 1:1). Readers answer this in several ways. Many argue that 1 Samuel describes where Elkanah lived rather than his tribe: Levites lived in towns throughout the other tribes, including Ephraim, as this chapter's own list of Levitical towns shows, so a Levite could be called an Ephraimite by where he lived. Others think Samuel's family was counted among the Levites because of his service, or that the Chronicler is expressing his role in Levitical terms. The first explanation fits the chapter's own information, and it has many defenders. Either way, Samuel's service at the tabernacle fits the Chronicler's picture of him within the tribe that served God's house.
passages.asks: The priestly line ran through exile and out the other side. Ask what has carried your faith through a time when everything else was lost. And ask whose faithful service, unnoticed by most, has kept worship going where you are.

passages.t: The singers, the work of atonement, and the Levites' towns
passages.happening:
‘These are the men David put in charge of the music in the house of the LORD after the ark rested there’ (verse 31). They served with song before the tent of meeting until Solomon built the temple (verse 32). Heman's family tree is traced back to Levi, with Asaph at his right hand and Ethan at his left (verses 33-47).

‘Their fellow Levites were assigned to every kind of service of the tabernacle, the house of God’ (verse 48). ‘But Aaron and his sons did all the work of the Most Holy Place. They presented the offerings on the altar of burnt offering and on the altar of incense to make atonement for Israel’ (verse 49). The chapter ends with the towns given to the Levites throughout the tribes, with their pasturelands (verses 54-81).
passages.hearers:
The singers' family trees run backward, from the singer to Levi, as if climbing the tree. Heman stands in the center with Asaph on his right and Ethan on his left, the arrangement of a choir. Chronicles gives music a dignity other historical books do not: singing in worship is an office, with families appointed and trained for it.

Only Aaron's descendants offered sacrifices, burned incense and served in the Most Holy Place to make atonement. The word, kipper, means to cover, cleanse or ransom, removing what separates a people from God so that he can live among them. In the Old Testament atonement is God's provision through the sacrifices he appointed, not a human attempt to buy his favor. The other Levites did every other kind of service, and the word for it, avodah, can mean both labor and worship.

The Levites had no tribal land. The LORD himself was their portion, and they lived from the people's tithes and offerings. Instead they received towns scattered through all the tribes, with the pastureland around them, which spread God's servants through Israel. The list closely follows Joshua 21. Some of the towns were cities of refuge, where a person who had killed someone by accident could find protection until a proper judgment; Hebron and Shechem are named among them.
passages.later: The LORD told Aaron, ‘I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites’ (Numbers 18:20). Hebrews says of Jesus that ‘He sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself’ (Hebrews 7:27), and Paul urges believers to ‘sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts to God’ (Colossians 3:16).
passages.asks: Some carried, some guarded, some sang, and some made atonement, and all of it was service to God. Ask what your part is in the worship of God's people. And ask whether you treat ordinary work as service too.
